name: Okta: many MFA push challenges for one user (MFA fatigue)
description: Five or more Okta Verify push challenges sent to the same user within one rule run (about 5 minutes). This pattern suggests someone who has the password is flooding the user with pushes, hoping one gets approved. Built from the Sigma rule okta/okta_mfa_push_fatigue.yml; the threshold is applied here.
author: Lucas Gundry
false_positives: A user whose phone is offline or slow, retrying several times. Check for denials (there usually are none) and ask the user.
An app or script retrying a sign-in that triggers a push. Check user_agent.original and whether the pushes are evenly spaced.
note:
## What this rule counts
Okta Verify push challenges sent (`system.push.send_factor_verify_push`), grouped by `user.name`. An attacker who already has the password sends push after push, hoping the user taps Approve to make it stop (MFA fatigue, or MFA bombing).

## Triage
- Who: `user.name`. Did they start these sign-ins? Ask them out of band (not by a channel the attacker might control).
- From where: `source.ip`, `source.geo.*`, `source.as.organization.name`. Known for this user?
- Denials: `user.authentication.auth_via_mfa` with `event.outcome: failure`, `okta.debug_context.debug_data.factor: OKTA_VERIFY_PUSH` and `okta.outcome.reason: INVALID_CREDENTIALS`, for the same user in the same minutes (checked on one live denial; Okta logged no `user.mfa.okta_verify.deny_push` event for a denial that wasn't reported as suspicious). Several denials make this much more likely to be an attack.
- What came next: an approved push (`user.authentication.auth_via_mfa` success) or a new session after the pushes is the case that matters. If so, treat the password as known to the attacker: reset it and revoke sessions (both need human approval).

## Timing
- Ingest time (`event.ingested`), so late events still count in the next run.

## Known limits
- Event name checked against real homelab events. The 5-push threshold itself has not fired on real data.
- Slow drip: one push every 10 minutes never reaches 5 in one lookback. A companion rule on denials, or a longer window, would catch it.
- The threshold of 5 is a starting value, not tuned against real traffic.
- Number matching (Okta Verify asking the user to pick a number) makes blind approval much harder; this rule still matters for orgs or policies without it.

## Field mapping from Sigma
The query is the Sigma rule converted with `sigma convert -t lucene -p pipelines/okta-ecs.yml`; the threshold is added here.
- `eventtype` -> `event.action`
- logsource `okta` -> `event.dataset: okta.system`
